name: Vera Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computer science with a data focus, so my week is half lectures and half me trying things on my laptop. On Wednesdays I do a hackathon night with a few friends, and on weekends I build small websites for local shops, which pays about 150 a month. I share a flat with two other students, and my parents cover the rent and a bit more. Dad runs a dairy farm and Mum is a vet nurse, so I grew up around actual living things and I'm quite glad to be near screens now. I use AI tools every day, for code, for planning my week, even for deciding what to cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, as long as people stop expecting miracles. To friends I'd say it's a normal tool that's useful in a hundred small ways, like spreadsheets were. At the hackathon I'd say fine, then we build things with what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. My path stays the same: degree, internship, junior job. I'd lose a bit of my edge, since I use the tools more than most, but I'd still be ahead on skills. The thing I worry about in this world is rural money: the farm margins, and milk prices swinging about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on exactly as I am: do the degree, keep building small sites for shops, and enter hackathons. I'd try to turn the website work into something steadier, like a monthly care plan for the shops. I'd also ask Dad to let me build him a simple herd-records tool, since he still uses a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just a normal student life, and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farm. How worried are you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only in the normal way. Dad's farm has been in the family for three generations, and milk prices go up and down. He says the farm will see me through, but I don't want to need it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the herd-records tool do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Track which cow was treated, when, and by whom, so Dad doesn't hunt through paper. A herd-records tool sounds boring, but it saves my dad about an hour a day, which is the thing farmers don't have.

say: It's a **normal tool**, useful in a hundred small ways, as long as people stop expecting miracles.
At the hackathon I'd say fine, and **build with what works**.
think: My path stays the same, though I'd lose a bit of my **edge** on the tools.

do: Keep building **small sites** for shops and turn it into monthly care plans.
Build my dad a **herd-records tool** to replace his paper diary.
feel: **Calm**, a normal student life that I like.

steps.text: Offer local shops a monthly website care plan
Build a herd-records tool for my dad's dairy farm
Keep entering the Wednesday hackathon nights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is where the game gets interesting. To friends I'd say learn the tools well, and learn what's underneath, so you're the person who spots the mistakes. Online I'd write about the middle path: don't panic, don't gloat, just keep your skills up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm in a good position, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't make me careful. Juniors who do routine coding are the ones who feel it first, and I don't want to be a routine coder. I'd want to be the person who understands the business and uses the tools as a team of helpers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the tools harder and learn how to build with them, like pipelines that check each other's work. I'd go for a placement at a company with real data, maybe in a lab or in agriculture. And I'd keep the freelance work, since it forces me to talk to actual customers, which is the part nobody can automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. A bit like surfing: scary until you're up on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle most in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who stopped learning. My friend's older brother is a junior accountant, and his firm has stopped hiring juniors. He's good, but he's the type who waits to be told. I'd say that waiting is the risky part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you help someone like him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer, yes. I'd say here's a weekend project, let's build a small tool for the firm's invoices. Showing someone they can do it is better than telling them they should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to start working out the rules now, because this will hit before institutions can react. To friends I'd say panicking isn't a plan, but neither is pretending it's normal. I'd put up a short post saying I'm preparing and I'd ask if others are too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite shaken. If AI does almost any thinking work by 2028, the job I'm studying for might not exist when I'm done. I'm adaptive, but this is different, because my skills are exactly what gets replaced. The farm is an anchor, because food and animals are hands-on, and robots need three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about where I'd land if the screen work vanished. I'd probably ask Dad to teach me the farm's operations, because understanding how a business runs matters more than coding. I'd keep the freelance work, save as much as I can, and talk to my parents about their own plans. Then I'd look at being the person who connects AI to farms, since a farm is a place where hands-on and thinking work meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit like being a fast swimmer in a river where the current just got ten times stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say that to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, over a phone call on Sunday. Mum would go quiet and then ask practical questions. Dad would say the cows still need milking, which is both comforting and not at all helpful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My spending. I'd stop the little things, like takeaway and the streaming service. And I'd start a proper emergency fund, even 30 a week. If I have six months of runway, I can make clear decisions.

Panicking isn't a plan, but neither is pretending it's **normal**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is just enough to build something useful, if we start now. To friends I'd say pick a problem you care about and attach yourself to it, because the people who matter in 2031 will be the ones who know a field deeply and know the tools. I'd also say don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel energised and a bit nervous. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030, and by then I'd have two years of side projects and maybe a first customer. It's a race, but one I can enter, because I'm already comfortable with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend my summers on real placements. I'd keep building the farm tool and try to sell it to ten farms, not just Dad. I'd also look for a part-time role with a company that works on AI in agriculture or health. And I'd save around 4,000, so I have a cushion when 2031 arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy, a bit like the night before a long trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why agriculture or health?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because those are fields where hands-on work and thinking work meet, and where robots take longer than 2031. If I'm the one who understands both a cow and a database, I'm useful for a while longer than someone who only does one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the plan fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pivot. I'm not precious about it. A plan is a draft, and I change drafts all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people will probably change plans several times. To friends I'd say stay curious and don't marry one skill. At the hackathon I'd say let's build something now, and we can worry about 2036 later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. I'd be 28, with some savings, a few years of work, and maybe my own company. If the thinking work goes in 2036 I'd have the edge of knowing the tools and a field. I'd worry a little about my parents, since Dad will be in his sixties on a farm that's heavy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a couple of years at a small team, and try to start something around farms or health. I'd use my first salaries to help my parents put in more automation, like milking robots or better records. And I'd keep learning a new tool every few months, because by then that's just life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It's not going to catch me off guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay near the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I think I'd move to a city for the first few years, for the jobs, then maybe come back, working remotely or running something nearby. I'd like the idea of living near open ground again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Support for small businesses to adopt the tools, so it's not only giant firms. And training that's open to everybody, including farmers like my dad. If it's only the young who get ready, that's a failure.

say: Ten years is long, so **stay curious** and don't marry one skill.
I'd say let's **build something now** and worry about 2036 later.
think: I'd be **calm**: 28, with savings, a few years of work, and maybe my own company.
I'd worry a little about my **parents**, because dairy farming is heavy work in their sixties.

Use early salaries to help my parents add **automation**.
Learn a **new tool** every few months.
feel: **Calm and curious**, not likely to be caught off guard.
S4.quote: If it's only the young who get ready, that's a failure.
fieldNote: Sees the **long horizon** as normal life: keep learning, stay flexible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, since I'd have no time to build the cushion, the company or the experience. I'd still be a student, and my parents would be at risk too. What would help is quick public training, easy tools for small businesses, and honest information about where the work actually moves. And a loan system that doesn't punish people for changing their course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that adaptive doesn't mean fearless. I use the tools every day and I still lie awake thinking about it sometimes. I just try to turn the worry into a small action before it gets big.

headlineQuote: Adaptive doesn't mean fearless. I use the tools every day and I still lie awake thinking about it sometimes.
portrait: Vera is an **18-year-old** computer science student with a data focus, who builds websites for shops and uses AI every day.
Her dad runs a **dairy farm** and her mum is a vet nurse, which makes farming her anchor and her opportunity.
She is a pragmatic centrist who aims for the **overlap** of hands-on and thinking work, like farms and health.
She is calm in slower worlds and **anxious at two years**, where she turns worry into cuts, savings and a plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most: no time to build a cushion, a company or experience, and her parents at risk too.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **public training**, easy tools for small businesses, honest information on where work moves, and a loan system that allows course changes.
